Building on cutting-edge experimental projects such as HIBEF at the XFEL, our calculations investigate the detection of quantum vacuum effects including diffraction and birefringence. By utilizing a helically polarized x-ray beam, we can distinguish between the rates of photon transmission with opposite polarizations, thus enabling the detection of a shift in the wavelength that is purely rotational. Furthermore, our study demonstrates that special detector configurations can significantly enhance detection capabilities, allowing for an amplification of birefringent effects by a factor of 1000 through coherent detection with a crystal, while in random detection this effect is reduced. Additionally, we find that optimal detector configurations lead to a substantial reduction of diffraction-related photon deviations, effectively confining photons to traverse minimal distances from their initial trajectory.

This note outlines the algorithm devised by J. M. Eisenlohr and S. L. Farris to
systematically generate all fully transitive polyhedra in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space. Furthermore, this algorithm is employed to construct a novel polyhedron within three-dimensional Euclidean space.

Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. This property is a significant advancement over traditional clone-resistant cryptography. We have revisited and expanded the definitions, constructions, and applications of unclonable encryption introduced in 2012, simplifying some of the existing methods based on their basic idea. We have also explored several new directions, including fully secure multicopy-unclonable encryption using MC-PUFE, a connection between clone-resistant encryption and unclonable encryption, and a secure voting protocol built on unclonable encryption.

This study confirms that physical layer authentication in mobile communications is viable under standard signal conditions, obviating the need for secret keys. We demonstrate that a simple, effective algorithm can accurately distinguish authorized devices from impostors in telephone line transmissions, outperforming existing keyless methods. Furthermore, this algorithm's universal application across various communication media, combined with its cost efficiency, makes it an alternative to cryptographic layers in secure data transfer.

We utilized the flat bands within the moiré superlattices of twisted transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) to investigate plasmons through self-consistent calculations that incorporated electromagnetic interactions. Our findings indicate that at carrier fillings corresponding to the valleys of the flat bands, plasmons experience a significant increase in energy due to interaction effects. Notably, when nested conditions are not satisfied, flat-band plasmons are predicted to emerge within the single-layer TMDs, and these excitations may be observable through inelastic electron scattering. Furthermore, due to in-plane phonon coupling, these plasmons are expected to result in a distinct feature in Raman spectra, particularly in regions where plasmons satisfy nested conditions only, creating an asymmetric pattern. This work paves the way for further exploration and verification using inelastic electron scattering, phonon scattering, and Raman spectroscopy.

This paper expresses the potential function $f$ associated with an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold in terms of the scalar field $p$, determining when the potential function is constant, and establishing a link between $f$ and $\frac{df}{dt}$. We also derive a formula for $\Delta f$ and prove that a Ricci soliton on a shrinking Sasakian manifold is Ricci flat if it is almost conformal. Consequently, we establish that any shrinking Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold is Ricci flat. Additionally, we verify that any expanding Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold is Ricci flat.

Both celestial bodies can experience mass loss due to an expansive outer layer, 
which can be driven or hindered by strong magnetic fields. This phenomenon occurs 
in various forms across different types of stars and planets. Mass loss can take the 
form of a widespread outflow, as seen in some types of stars, or in both stars and 
gas giants, it can be shaped into twisted magnetic fields that create star-shaped 
magnetospheres. The extent and composition of these magnetospheres can vary greatly, 
affecting the surrounding environment and impacting both the stellar and planetary 
systems. This, in turn, can influence the development of atmospheres and the potential 
for habitability in some types of stars and planets.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect (SOPE) is a phenomenon that occurs when a material with strong spin-orbit coupling is brought into contact with another, making its electrons exhibit SO properties. In this study, we present theoretical predictions for the size and length scales of the SOPE in cobalt/bismuth multilayer structures, examining how the layers interact and the scattering at their interface influences the Johnbar-Oplem effect. By combining accurate models with actual measurements of resistivity, we found that even very thin cobalt layers can exhibit significant SOPE, with a large effective spin-orbit field of about 10 mT generated at a specific bismuth layer thickness of 4 nm. This finding holds the potential for enhancing the efficiency of magnetic memory devices that utilize SO components.

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha}+B/r^{\alpha}+C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using a fractional form of the Adomian polynomial method, we obtained solutions that also relate to previously reported results based on different approaches. Furthermore, our technique successfully applies to fractional cases, demonstrating its versatility.

We investigate a novel approach to improving neural network performance by adopting a strategy inspired by control theory, specifically by incorporating a Lipschitz constraint. This ensures that the network's output changes are limited, which aligns with robustness against external perturbations. To achieve this, we modify the standard optimization objective used in training, by introducing a constraint that limits the gradient of the network. This can be effectively addressed using the activation reformulation technique, leading to a modification of the optimization problem. As a result, there is a clear relationship between penalty and constraint-based methods for regularisation, with penalty-based method emerging as an approximation of the latter. Empirical evidence obtained through numerical experiments indicates that directly enforcing the Lipschitz constraint yields superior results compared to applying a penalty, especially when the imposed penalty is relatively high.

Sequential neural network models have seen significant success in handling language understanding tasks, particularly with the long short-term memory (LSTM) architecture. Previous research has indicated that sequential models may struggle to process the grammatical complexities of languages, although some languages contain useful contextual elements, such as agreement, that could aid their comprehension. This study focuses on Basque, a language notable for its suffix-based inflectional system and its core requirement of verb-noun agreement. We conducted an experiment using the Basque BAbAr task, which tests the understanding of noun phrase antecedents in the verb. Our findings revealed that noun phrase-verb agreement in Basque is relatively straightforward, as both sequential and non-sequential models, including BiLSTM and BERT, achieved comparable high levels of performance. These results suggest that Basque may not be the most suitable language for detecting the distinctive advantages and disadvantages associated with processing sequential information within neural network models.

Astronomical observations of planets orbiting their stars are significantly hampered by stellar activity. Consequently, astronomers are developing new techniques to time these observations to minimize the effects of the star's brightness fluctuations. With the advent of the James Webb Space Telescope, almost all planetary discoveries in our galaxy will be made using this powerful instrument. However, the parent stars of these planets are often much more active than the stars that host known exoplanets. As a result, astronomers will need to carefully plan observations of these planets to maximize their success. To demonstrate the process of designing these missions, researchers selected HD 80606 b, a planet that orbits its relatively active star in an eccentric path. By analyzing archival observations of this planet with a global network of telescopes, researchers were able to create a highly accurate map of its orbit, which revealed that upcoming JWST observations can be perfectly timed to take advantage of its efficiency while avoiding the fluctuations in the star's brightness. Furthermore, researchers showed that this method of scheduling observations can be applied to a wide range of planets that orbit their stars in both circular and highly elliptical paths.

The success of engaging therapy relies on models that connect gameplay features to user feedback, which also guides rehabilitation system improvements. This study explores the application of data-driven approaches in physiotherapy, utilizing physio games as a example. It demonstrates how basic gameplay designs can be modified to meet the needs of patients undergoing rehabilitation, which can be further developed through advanced modeling techniques. Specifically, it discusses utilizing metrics like those from connective ensemble methods to identify how game changes affect patient motivation.

Our research offers a variational approximation, drawing from the Ambrosio-Tortorelli model, to quantify brittle fracture energies in complex, piecewise-rigid structures, applicable to both nonlinear and linearised elasticity frameworks.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan production of lepton-antiquark pairs and calculate precise predictions for this process including leading order quantum chromodynamic corrections. Our calculations, which are among the first of their kind, allow for reliable comparisons between theoretical predictions and experimental data, thereby providing a robust framework for identifying deviations from the Standard Model in lepton-flavour non-universality.

Recent advances in deep neural networks have significantly improved image reconstruction in Positron Emission Tomography (PET), enabling the utilization of auxiliary computed tomography (CT) and PET/CT data for partial-reconstruction of low-dose PET images. However, current deep learning-based methods often struggle to generalize effectively on test datasets that differ from training data due to variations in equipment, settings, and patient physiology. To overcome this limitation and achieve more consistent performance, we introduce a new approach that leverages prior PET and CT data to improve the reconstruction of low-dose PET images, while accounting for uncertainty in deep neural network outputs. Specifically, we employ a stochastic multi-task variational autoencoder to reconstruct low-dose PET images and generate corresponding CT data from partial PET inputs. We then develop a classification network that determines the uncertainty of PET/CT data based on a three-way decision mechanism. We also incorporate a robust loss function to minimize the impact of inaccurate three-way predictions. We train this uncertainty-aware multi-modal network using synthetic low-dose PET datasets and demonstrate its ability to produce accurate and consistent results.

The issue of tailoring news content to individual users while respecting their data has long plagued the industry. Although the personalization of online news feeds is now commonplace, there is a significant challenge in balancing user privacy. A proposed solution, called NPM - the Note to Myself framework, allows for highly personalized content without breaching user privacy. By leveraging secure computation, NPM enables users to engage with content that is both personal and confidential, without revealing their profile to third parties.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations develops, based on the concept of "focus" from information gradient analysis. The traditional explanation for coreferential use of pronouns in information gradient terms is closely linked to CT and the concept of focus. To examine the individual components of CT separately, we developed a system that adapts to the context of sentence processing and predicts the "focus" of the next sentence. We generated test cases to verify if the predicted "focus" matches the use of pronouns to refer back to entities. However, we found that simply applying CT to the context does not accurately predict coreferential pronoun usage. Additionally, when CT was combined with a more complex model of sentence processing, we obtained improved results, but only marginally significant. These findings suggest that CT, when used to represent context, may not be sufficient to explain the coherent nature of conversations.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel approach leverages structural properties of suitable graph classes, in combination with Sparsity Preserving Tree Decompositions and dynamic programming techniques.

The rising intricacy of modern adaptable systems demands elevated automation in their configuration process, thus also accelerating development cycles via rapid, automated workflow integration. A novel automated configuration framework is introduced, using model checking and SMT, adaptable to any domain definable by SMT formulas, allowing for modular scalability and improved understanding via graph visualization tools.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties of operators within the Heisenberg picture, and mutual information between those operators and the structure of their underlying Krylov spaces. By focusing on SU(1,1) and SU(2) algebras, we validate our theoretical framework through comparison with explicit time-evolved operators, and explore both their global and local entanglement characteristics. Notably, we discover that in many cases, the time behavior of Krylov complexity directly correlates with that of global entanglement measures, such as the moment of inertia.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for providing indoor localization and distance measurement between individuals. Researchers have developed various techniques to estimate these values based on signal strength, but their accuracy remains limited. To improve such estimation, a machine learning-based approach is widely used. However, before applying this method, multiple data sets must be collected at specific distances, making it challenging to accurately estimate them. In this study, we examine the effectiveness of different machine learning algorithms in estimating distance and evaluate their performance using the Indoor Distance Estimation data set. Our findings show that a combination of support vector regression and linear regression methods, known as SVR-LR, outperformed other algorithms, including advanced ones like random forest and gradient boosting. This hybrid method achieved the lowest average absolute error of 0.5 meters and lowest RMS error of 0.67 meters. To further enhance the method, we experimented with different data preprocessing methods and found that applying logarithmic transformation to the received signal strength improved the average absolute error to 0.42 meters and the lowest root mean square error to 0.58 meters for the SVR-LR model.

We explore a hypothetical scenario in astronomy where advanced civilizations, known as Type III, construct Dyson Spheres to harness a black hole's energy through a process called the Penrose Process. By applying an effective fluid theory to multiple particle systems, the complex behavior of these particles surrounding the black hole can be simplified. Our study calculates the equivalent "color temperature" of this system using fluid theory and compares its predictions with actual particle simulations, revealing that temperatures closer to the black hole are higher. This process also allows us to estimate the maximum amount of power that could be generated by a Dyson Sphere around a large, rotating black hole, even considering the energy losses caused by the particles themselves.

Network-based services are increasingly relied upon and, consequently, the identification of failures or deviations from agreed-upon performance standards has become critical. Although traditional methods exist to monitor these issues, they often involve significant costs or lack the flexibility of new approaches. One such method, which involves measuring performance at specific points, lacks the adaptability to accommodate the dynamic nature of modern services. This paper proposes an innovative approach to decentralized performance monitoring that leverages peer-to-peer technology. By utilizing this technology, we can achieve a more adaptable and cost-effective monitoring system that offers several advantages, including adaptability to dynamic services and the ability to pinpoint performance issues with high accuracy. Our approach is illustrated through the example of web hosting services and is found to be a more efficient and flexible solution in performance monitoring.

The beam breakup instability poses a significant challenge to the design of particle accelerators, particularly those with high beam powers and short gaps, which are crucial for certain types of particles like superconducting cavities. To address this limitation and enable more complex and versatile research, a critical step is developing effective beam breakup control methods. This study focuses on understanding how different patterns of radio frequency power affect the beam breakup instability in energy recovery linacs. By analyzing both theoretical models and real-world data from actual runs, this study gains valuable insights into the phenomenon. The research also explores the possibility of using a specific type of feedback system, which takes into account the effects of the electric charges left behind by the beam, to suppress the beam breakup effect in energy recovery linacs.

To determine the parameters for neutrino oscillations, the GEONuVO experiment will analyze the neutron behavior in the GEOSTORE detector's scintillator bars following the GEOSTORE volume being irradiated by the CERN Neutrino discovery beam. The precision of the neutron signal identification and characterization is essential for this analysis. The GEONuVO detection setup comprises three NCT stations, each consisting of 128 custom-designed 3D-projection detectors. The beam's intensity and the neutron flux are measured using the 3D-projection detectors in the NCT1 and NCT2 stations, while the first interaction points of the neutrons are analyzed with the NCT3 station. The 3D-projection detectors are capable of detecting the time, position, and energy of hadronic interactions. The GEONuVO team has performed a comprehensive neutron simulation and measured the total cross-section of neutrons interacting with protons and carbon nuclei, based on data from the NCT1, NCT2, and NCT3 stations. The results of this study are presented to the GEONuVO collaboration.

In a previous study, research was conducted to observe the adhesion of model particles under various conditions, including different gases and temperatures. Now, the experiment was repeated with model particles preheated to the same temperatures used during the testing phase. Using the same molecular dynamics simulations, the researchers found that preheating the particles had no noticeable impact on their adhesion strength when the testing temperatures were room temperature or lower. However, preheating the particles to 300K and above resulted in a decrease in adhesion strength by a factor of 10 compared to particles tested at the same temperatures but prekept at room temperature. This finding suggests that the structural and thermal equilibrium of the particles is crucial to their adhesion strength. As these particles are now subjected to the high temperatures present in astrophysical settings, their sticking properties are significantly altered. As such, the sticking temperature limits for various models must be revised upwards. This study also marks the first molecular dynamics study to examine the adhesion of organic compounds with incorporated water molecules at high temperatures. The addition of water to the particles' surfaces led to their reconfiguration into compact, glass-like structures. This in turn led to their increased adhesion strength when the testing temperatures were below 400K. Conversely, above 400K, the incorporated water led to the particles' breakdown into less dense forms, which in turn decreased their adhesion strength.

Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) is a localized adaptation of the traditional Fisher Discriminant Analysis, widely employed for supervised dimensionality reduction techniques. The LFDA R package allows users to execute various LFDA methodologies, including different local connectivity strategies and evaluation tools, to determine the optimal parameters. This package also facilitates dimensionality reduction visualization through t-SNE and allows users to compare LFDA and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classification accuracies.

Imitation learning has gained significant attention in robotics due to its ability to enable robots to efficiently acquire complex behaviors from human demonstrations. While previous research on imitation learning has primarily focused on learning unconstrained demonstrations, many tasks in robotics require demonstrations that adhere to various constraints, including linear and nonlinear conic constraints, as well as time and space requirements. To address this limitation, we have developed unconstrained learning frameworks that incorporate a broad range of constrained demonstrations and allow for the learning models to adapt to the demonstrations. Furthermore, we have introduced an additional constraint, the avoidance of nonlinear obstacles in time and space. We have also extended our work to include multiple demonstrations that differ in their quality and timing. Experimental results from both simulated and real-world applications have shown the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning complex behaviors, including walking, swinging, swinging with an adjustable swing, and using a robotic arm to place an object in a target area.

To improve the precision of the particle colliders like LHC, understanding and reducing systematic uncertainties associated with jet measurements is crucial. A key factor in this understanding is accurately predicting how particles interact at collision points, specifically the emission vertex. This study directly calculates a specific quantum correction, represented by a one-loop trilinear interaction involving two gluons and an implicit scalar component, within the framework of N=4 super-Yang-Mills theory. This calculation employs an on-shell approach, utilizing anomalous dimensions of operator conformal multiplications to derive a 6x6 matrix of imaginary anomalous dimensions. This matrix encompasses interactions among various types of helicity-carrying particles. As a result, it yields a comprehensive expression for a one-loop correction, applicable to heavy-ion collisions and other particle interactions. This detailed representation includes contributions from both Yang-Mills and heavy-ion collisions, thus providing an essential component for refining theoretical predictions in high-energy particle physics.

A novel class of superconductors featuring spin-singlet pairing emerges from a balance between the Rashba interaction and an attractive Fermi interaction in the Hubbard-Rashba model. Using a mean-field approach, we've identified the conditions under which these spin-singlet pairings lead to topologically non-trivial phases characterized by a non-zero value of the invariant. Our calculations reveal that the topological nature of these superconductors can be manipulated by altering the Rashba interaction strength, and we propose using a monolayer of molybdenum disulfide as a platform to experimentally verify our predictions through measurements of edge conductance and the quantum spin Hall effect. Furthermore, we explore the effects of disorder on these phenomena using the self-consistent non-crossing approximation.

By utilizing a high magnetic field, a lattice of vortices has been created within a single-crystalline YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6.95}$ sample, which was then imaged via scanning tunneling microscopy. The resulting images revealed square-shaped vortices arranged in a square lattice structure, which was consistently maintained across various magnetic field strengths, from 30 to 60 Tesla. This observation, made possible by employing localized measurements, provides strong evidence for the existence of a square-square vortex lattice transition phase in this material.

Theories of molten polymer brushes have long been debated regarding their swelling and stress characteristics. Recent research has revealed significant discrepancies between the predictions of recent brush theories and those of Monte Carlo simulations, even in scenarios with high stretch levels. We present an innovative approach that bridges the gap between high and low stretch levels, allowing for the analysis of brushes in various geometries. Our method employs a stochastic approach that combines Monte Carlo simulations with local equilibrium assumptions, leading to a streamlined algorithm capable of efficiently generating the morphology of molten polymer brushes. Moreover, this method is not limited to one specific brush geometry and can be applied to a range of scenarios.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning in image processing, specifically with data from the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To demonstrate this approach, they employed classification algorithms to analyze 8 years of 0.3 GeV - 300 GeV time-differential energy spectra and spatially resolved images of the sky. By creating a binary map of the sky, they distinguished between regions with constant high-energy emission and regions without, using a area of the Milky Way as a test case. Traditional analysis showed a significant difference between the areas with constant high-energy emission and those without. However, when examining the areas with high-energy emission using a more sensitive K-fold cross-validation method, significant variations were revealed that differed from the conventional findings. These variations were linked to nearby radio sources, X-ray binaries, and other gamma-ray sources, which create complex patterns of high and low energy flux regions. This study paves the way for a unique approach in characterizing the spectral properties of gamma rays in the time-dependent 4D regime of the Fermi-LAT data.

Inspired by the efficiency of Nash Equilibria in cooperative games, researchers aim to extend this work to cooperative games where not all agents are equally influential. We investigate a class of cooperative games where agents act in a fixed sequence, making decisions based on prior actions, and demonstrate that an optimal order of action leads agents to reach a cooperative equilibrium that surpasses Nash Equilibria in certain scenarios. We develop algorithms to efficiently find the best sequence of action for a given set of agents and a limited number of underlying cooperative equilibria, and provide theoretical bounds on the complexity of this problem, including its NP-hardness when agents can be divided into two equal groups.

We develop a method to identify binary asteroids in images by analyzing their light curves, adapting an existing algorithm for variable star detection. This approach involves comparing the movement of an asteroid to that of other celestial objects and pinpointing anomalies caused by an asteroid orbiting its binary partner. Our tests show the algorithm can accurately detect asteroid binaries and provide an upper limit for the minimum size of a small asteroid in such systems. Using our method on Pan-STARRS1 images, analyzed by the PS1-VARCA team, we identified two potential binary asteroids and contributed to the discovery of another, designated 2012 SB190, as of July 2018. Furthermore, our study establishes a size limit for the small asteroid in close systems with periods under one day and a diameter of at least 0.3 kilometers.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper's first section explores the asymptotic behavior of the estimators presented in section 2 of the Auerbach's work. The second section investigates extensions to the model. The third section applies the model to estimate peer effects within networks. The fourth section presents results obtained from simulated data.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, five quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and five chain rule formulas have been established.

This paper analyzes the performance of complex MIMO systems that utilize spatial modulation and multiuser detection with a least-squares method, and derives rate and distortion metrics for this setup. By applying an asymptotic characterization, we evaluate specific detector methods, including an optimal Bayesian detector, and develop a simplified approach for optimizing a related detection method, before supporting our findings with numerical simulations.

We've developed an open-source suite of web visualization tools tailored for
analyzing spectral and imaging data, which are being utilized in the second edition
of the RCSED galaxy group catalog (http://rcsed2.astr0.edu/). This group catalog
contains nearly 2000 long-slit spectra, and we've applied a novel, semi-automatic
method to create velocity maps of the galaxy group's members. We've demonstrated
that this approach can efficiently process up to 2000 spectra in about 5 minutes,
yielding high-quality, redshift measurements for the spectra. To achieve this, we
have developed a set of web visualization tools that not only facilitate the
creation of quality assessments, galaxy classifications, and error analyses from
raw chi-square fits, but also provide a framework for generating velocity spectra
and exploring their characteristics. Additionally, these tools are designed to be
accessible to non-programmers through a user-friendly interface, and the source
code is available on GitHub (https://github.com/RCSED/rcsed-web-tools-v2).

The South Atlantic rift system, which spans from the Equator to the Southern Atlantic, is composed of distinct segments with varying characteristics. These segments are divided into three zones: the Equatorial Volcanic Province, the Central Atlantic Shear Zone, and the South Atlantic Volcanic Province. The Central Atlantic Shear Zone exhibits extensive crustal thinning, while the northern and southern portions of this zone show continental extension. The two volcanic provinces, located to the north and south of the shear zone, are characterized by localized melting of the lithospheric mantle, which is marked by widespread flood basalts. These two provinces are further divided into two sectors, each with its own strike-slip fault system. The Central Atlantic Shear Zone acts as a barrier between these fault systems, which are oriented in opposite directions. The two fault systems within the Central Atlantic Shear Zone are marked by extensive normal faulting, which is evident in the central part of this zone. A prominent problem in medical image analysis is boundary accuracy.  To improve medical image segmentation quality, a self-supervised learning technique proposed recently, Information Maximization, utilizes an encoder without a decoder to efficiently utilize a large amount of unannotated data.  However, research indicates that some features identified by this method are not precise at the boundaries.  To address this issue, an innovative approach called Boundary-aware Information Maximization is developed.  This approach selects highly informative and boundary-accurate features for pre-training by incorporating a guided self-supervised learning strategy and a new criterion called feature stability.  To validate the method, comprehensive experiments were performed on public datasets including U-Net training based on BMML and MM liver MRI.  Results show that BAM outperforms current state-of-the-art self-supervised learning techniques and significantly surpasses traditional med. information maximization training methods.  Therefore, BAM is a powerful approach for public datasets and private CT/MRI with sparse training labels.

We introduce a novel approach to conversational guidance through a new framework, a new AI model, and a corresponding dataset, specifically tailored for role-playing games like Dungeons and Dragons. Our theory-of-mind-based model learns to communicate with team members and a player, aiming to help them reach shared objectives. This model is capable of inferring the goals of other participants, formulating strategies to achieve them, and leading the group towards desired outcomes. It was trained using reinforcement learning in collaboration with a simulated Dungeons and Dragons party, consisting of a human player, AI-controlled enemies, and a pre-established world scenario. Our significant achievement is that our model, assigned a specific role within the group, learned to negotiate with others, set goals, and lead the team to success. It was capable of making a substantial impact on the group's performance, leading to a substantial improvement in reward acquisition. However, our model is limited to small-scale scenarios and specific roles within the group. To overcome these challenges, we outline several potential avenues for future research. Notably, our approach and dataset can be applied to other domains that involve cooperative problem-solving, such as robotics and virtual reality simulations.

Despite significant research on Lexical Semantic Change Detection, most approaches remain limited to standard model assessments. This study deviates from this focus, shifting towards change discovery - identifying previously unknown word meanings emerging over time within a comprehensive corpus vocabulary. By extensively fine-tuning both a type-based and a token-based methodology on German datasets, our work showcases their applicability in discovering new words with evolving meanings. Additionally, our proposed framework is designed for nearly full automation of both evaluation and discovery processes.

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon, which can be described using operator product expansion and Wilson line formalism, and have implications in x-gluon scattering using the collinear factorization theorem.

The complex relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is not fully understood. Recent research has revealed that some knotted proteins evolve rapidly, sharing a common ancestor with the signal peptide region. To shed light on the connection between protein knots and their folding mechanisms, we developed a mathematical approach to analyze protein structure data. By examining the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms in various proteins, we identified potential folding pathways. Our method revealed that many knotted proteins have a specific sequence of structures that guide them toward their final shape. Analysis of 14 proteins with different knot types and signal peptides showed that most of these proteins follow a particular order of transformations to form their knots. In contrast, some unknotted proteins showed more diverse folding patterns. This research provides insights into the factors that influence the folding mechanisms of knotted proteins.

To resolve the discrepancy in the Hubble constant measurement, early dark energy is proposed as a solution. This theory's primary requirement is to delay the moment when the universe transitions from expansion to contraction, which could be achieved through the introduction of early dark energy in the universe's structure formation process. This study presents the most precise measurements of the early dark energy's influence, made with data from Planck and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey. By utilizing the maximum likelihood method, we place a constraint on the energy density of early dark energy relative to the critical density of the universe, which, when combined with evidence from the supernovae survey, results in the constraint denoted as $\Omega_{\rm EDE} f_{\rm EDE}^2/ m_{\rm pl}^2 < 0.84$ at the 95% confidence level.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite.

A detailed analysis of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken using the effective action approach in both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories. In our study, we first apply a general proof based on the exact Ward-Takahashi (WT) identities, which constitutes a primary objective. A secondary goal involves showcasing how a specific set of NG modes arises, which can be demonstrated through an analysis of NG mode dispersion and their corresponding spacetime patterns, which we achieve through both effective field theory (EFT) and lattice simulations. We begin our proof by establishing the exact WT identities, which are derived from the path integral formulation. A key step in our proof is establishing a precise relationship between NG modes and the pole positions of the partial wave amplitudes, which constitutes a key finding. A crucial observation is that the dispersion pattern of NG modes is solely determined by the NG-NG scattering amplitudes at threshold, which is only possible due to the exact WT identities. We further demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to the chiral perturbation theory (ChPT), where we confirm the existence of the NG triangle and analyze its angular patterns in both the relativistic and nonrelativistic contexts. We also provide an example using lattice simulations, which further corroborates our theoretical predictions.

Recent studies indicate that augmenting training data with counterfactual examples can significantly enhance classification models' robustness to adversarial inputs while improving their accuracy and efficiency. Notably, generating high-quality counterfactual data that maintain semantic similarity to original samples but result in different class predictions is a challenging task. To accomplish this, we explore the use of generative models in conjunction with a strong classification model to: (1) randomly generate phrasal counterfactuals from a vast vocabulary and (2) select the most effective counterfactuals that lead to a different class prediction. We investigate the use of the classification model in two ways to rank the generated phrasal data, including using it to maximize the difference between counterfactual and original samples' distances to the class center and to classify the counterfactuals into the target class with a low confidence level. We apply our method to multiple downstream tasks and evaluate the impact of various generators and vocabulary sizes on the resulting counterfactual data on downstream classification tasks. Our findings show that using phrasal counterfactuals generated and selected with the help of a strong classifier yields an increase in efficiency and a decrease in computational costs when using linear models, resulting in a significant improvement in model performance with a decrease in errors when evaluated with standard benchmarks.

In this study, we determined the total chromatic numbers along with their equitable and
neighborhood sum distinguishing counterparts for specific types of circulant graphs.

Research into remote epitaxy on graphene has been largely hindered by insufficient understanding of its underlying mechanisms. To address this, we explored the rare phenomenon of remote epitaxy in highly lattice-mismatched systems, specifically the 31% mismatch between cubic Heusler compounds and hexagonal graphene. We examined two Heusler materials, Cu2MnSn and Cu2SnSe3, which can be epitaxially grown on graphene via remote, pinhole, or van der Waals epitaxy, respectively. Utilizing a combination of experimental techniques and theoretical calculations, we investigated how strain and electronic effects influence the growth of these films. We observed that remote epitaxy is favored when there is a moderate lattice mismatch, whereas highly mismatched systems require an analysis of competing strain and electronic factors. We developed a method to predict remote epitaxy based on these factors and experimentally verified it. We also identified the unique properties of graphene that can be engineered to control the balance between remote epitaxy and other forms of epitaxy, providing a pathway for precise control over the growth of complex, highly lattice-mismatched films.

A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that arises from the combination of $\Z_p$ and $\Z_{p^2}$-linear components through the use of a specific ring $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$. For the purpose of understanding the properties of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes, researchers have investigated two key attributes: rank and kernel of the underlying code, and found that several characteristics of these codes can be better comprehended by analyzing the rank and kernel of their parent code structures.

The technology of graded viscosity banks, specifically tapering, has been analyzed for its impact on polymer injection methods. Researchers have compared polynomial and log functions to determine which can replace traditional linear polymer slug designs, considering various end-of-displacement velocities. Numerical simulations were conducted using the PECAM polymer displacement model to evaluate these functions, focusing on velocity changes, polymer residence times, and cost-effectiveness. Results revealed that certain polynomial functions, such as cubic and higher-order sequences, can achieve velocity outcomes similar to log functions while providing more flexibility in selecting functions based on cost considerations. This study demonstrates that optimal polymer injection designs using graded viscosity banks can be highly effective in reducing polymer costs and residence times, with certain functions outperforming others in terms of cost-efficiency and performance.

Conditional GANs have achieved remarkable success in image segmentation tasks due to their ability to utilize contextual information. However, their reliance on precise, frame-by-frame labeling poses a significant burden on data annotation. To alleviate this issue, researchers have explored the use of single labels to train segmenters, but this approach often results in overestimation of target areas. Our investigation into a large dataset of time-series images reveals that most images are actually labeled with multiple tags, despite being annotated as single-label data. We developed an algorithm to automatically identify and extract multi-label labeled samples from single-label labeled datasets, and found that these samples can serve as superb training sets for segmenters that operate on single labels. When we combined a small set of multi-label samples with a large set of single-label data and trained a conditional segmentation model, it achieved near perfect accuracy, demonstrating its capability to accurately handle images with only a single label.

This research provides an upper bound for the energy associated with time-fractional phase-field equations, specifically demonstrating that a scaled difference between the current state and a reference state at earlier times is equivalent to the energy, as established by Challis in 1982, for both integer and non-integer values of time $\tau$. We verify this bound numerically for both time and spatial dimensions, employing a numerical method based on the Grunwald-Lietnikov approximation to solve the time-fractional derivative, and present detailed results from these experiments.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction is analogous to a mathematical procedure known as a left adjoint functor, specifically within the framework of category theory. This similarity extends to complex operations involving multiple states and algebras, resulting in combinations of Hilbert spaces and algebra elements. A particular emphasis is placed on the intricate combinatorial relationships that arise from this adjunction. We illustrate how a specific property known as the weak monotone property can be comprehended through a specific combinatorial structure, the 1-truncated cleavage, and prove its invariance under isomorphic transformations. Moreover, we establish a connection between algebraic elements and a specific type of operator and explore the underlying combinatorial structure of this relationship.

We propose a novel theory to explain high-energy gamma-rays found in energy ranges of 0.1-3 GeV in nearby radio galaxies and elliptical galaxies with radio emissions. Our hypothesis centers on magnetically arrested disks (MADs) in the central super-critical accretion disks of these galaxies' active galactic nuclei. 3D simulations of particle acceleration within MADs reveal the production of gamma-rays through interactions of high-energy particles with the surrounding matter, resulting in a significant gamma-ray emission that matches observed data. The predicted gamma-ray properties, including their energy distribution and brightness, are consistent with those of a generic active galactic nucleus model, providing a robust means of identifying MADs in future observations. Compared to the magnetic field within the jet, the field within the disk exhibits greater gamma-ray emission due to its interaction with surrounding cosmic dust and gas. Notably, our simulations also indicate that high-energy gamma-rays produced within the disk are confined, whereas lower energy radiation escapes freely. This confinement effect is further amplified by Compton scattering, which also modifies the predicted X-ray and infrared components of this multi-wavelength composite. The amount of Compton reflection observed in such systems may exceed that typically associated with the broad-line region in active galactic nuclei. Moreover, the predicted radio emissions in such systems are also consistent with observations, although further studies are required to determine their precise characteristics.

This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods for key areas in portfolio management, specifically targeting the efficient frontier and portfolio return distribution. We leverage recent theoretical advancements in probability, including heavy-tailed and fractional geometry, to develop cutting-edge algorithms for these applications. Leveraging these efficient methods, we can accurately predict portfolio returns, Leverageable Score, and VaR, and develop cutting-edge portfolio optimization techniques that consider both return and risk. Our proposed algorithm yields optimal solutions that are computationally feasible, and can be used to construct portfolios with ideal return distributions.

Early detection of heart conditions relies heavily on accurate stethoscope listening tests, making it crucial to achieve high levels of precision in this process. However, using digital recording devices to capture sound from stethoscopes can be hindered by noise from various sources, including the heart condition itself and the sensor. To overcome this challenge, deep learning models have the potential to learn to cope with these types of interference during training. Building on previous work, this study explores different deep learning approaches for analyzing heart sounds, with a focus on improving the efficiency of models used in this process. Through the use of reduced models and an updated dataset, this study demonstrates that careful selection of models and use of efficient training methods can lead to more precise results, outperforming approaches used in previous studies.

The proliferation of smartphones and smartphones-enabled devices has enabled health monitoring systems to collect valuable data on individuals' daily activities, including their location, communication patterns, and physical activity. This has led to the development of advanced health monitoring systems capable of making critical predictions about users' behavior and state, including their driving habits, activity levels, and risk of neurological disorders. Despite their benefits, these systems face significant challenges related to privacy concerns and data security when deploying learning algorithms on wearable devices. To address these issues, a federized healthcare learning framework called FedHealth has been proposed, which incorporates smartphone and wearable device technology to support activity recognition, classification, and health risk prediction through a hybrid federized and transfer learning approach. This approach allows for the creation of robust prediction models that can be personalized to individual users without compromising their personal data.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations.

We employ a quantum field theory approach to examine the long-term behavior of the universe's expansion, focusing on the universe's stochastic history. By representing the universe's random journey through the parameter space of scalar fields using a geometric path, we can calculate the probability of observing a particular cosmological event. This method, known as pasting conjecture, enables us to determine the probability measure for the universe's history. Investigating two scalar field models, we calculate the coincidence probability in each case. The analysis reveals that in both scenarios, the probability of the universe experiencing a particular coincidence event is governed by the exponential growth rate of the corresponding quantum field theory solution. The coincidence event's magnitude is determined by the difference in growth rates between the event and a reference event. The theoretical predictions are then compared to current cosmological observations. The analysis shows that the current universe's expansion rate is influenced by the maximum entropy state of the quantum field theory, and that the coincidence event's magnitude is determined by the difference in entropy between the event and a reference event. The maximum entropy state of the quantum field theory corresponds to a de Sitter universe, and that the coincidence event's magnitude is determined by the difference in entropy between the de Sitter universe and a reference universe. The analysis also shows that the current universe's expansion rate is influenced by the coincidence event's magnitude, and that the coincidence event's magnitude is determined by the difference in entropy between the event and a reference event. In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing numerous job applicants to select the best fit for available positions. This process can be significantly streamlined by automatically phoning interviewees, playing a standardized interview, and even PHAs. We present a method to automate parts of an organization's recruitment process. This approach includes playing a standardized interview to multiple job applicants and PHAs to each interviewee. This method significantly reduces the time required for a vital organizational process and ensures consistency in execution. We demonstrate this method's effectiveness by implementing it in the customer service department of a major bank in Brazil. This implementation results in processing 10 times more customers per day compared to traditional methods, reducing intervention times by 90%. Additionally, it leads to a 20% reduction in hiring costs.

This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change abruptly over time. Our main achievement is to derive an explicit solution for this problem using quasi-variational inequalities, thereby confirming the existence of a smooth value function. Additionally, we apply the findings to a simpler model involving two states with time-dependent costs.

To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates asymmetric leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and aid in identifying its potential. Asymmetric production stands out from conventional methods as leptoquarks created in proton-proton collisions aren't opposite charges. To make this process possible, we outline the required conditions and list all relevant combinations of leptoquark groups that can create it. Furthermore, our studies in the Standard Model and its scalar extensions demonstrate how to integrate this process into reinterpretations of existing experiments and leptoquark creation studies.

Temporal sequence analysis involves using sequence data that changes over time for prediction purposes. Typically, the learning algorithms used for this purpose have been developed assuming a fixed number of features and a fixed dimensionality of the time series. Typically series have a low dimensionality and a relatively long history. In contrast, we are dealing with data that has a large number of features but a relatively short history. Specifically, we have no prior knowledge of which features are relevant. We are tackling this problem within a supervised learning context. We have experimented with several approaches for this problem. We have found that relevant features can be identified through supervised feature selection. Alternatively, we can employ neural networks that automatically identify relevant features. These methods have resulted in significant performance gains compared to simply averaging the time series.

We have developed a theoretical model to explain the low-level excitation of a specific set of atomic fine structure lines, specifically focusing on a particular line within the near-infrared spectrum. This line is commonly used to determine the amount of cold gas present in galaxies. Our analysis revealed that in the densest regions of a galaxy's molecular reservoir, collisions between atoms are the primary factor responsible for the line's formation. However, in the more diffuse regions, the interaction between electrons and atoms becomes significant. These atomic excitations are responsible for a significant line broadening effect observed in galaxies' spectra. This line broadening is correlated with a specific threshold of gas density. This finding has implications for the interpretation of galaxy spectra, particularly for determining the total amount of gas present. Using a line-based method, we were able to estimate the mass of gas present in a sample of star-forming galaxies, which showed a strong correlation with measurements made using a more traditional method involving radiative transfer modeling. This line-based method proved to be a more efficient alternative to the more computationally expensive traditional method.

We tackle the long-standing puzzle in particle physics by introducing a new class of particles called right-handed heavy quarks, or vectorlike quarks, whose properties must be consistent with observed data from the LHC. In order to resolve the puzzling discrepancies seen in certain weak interaction decays, these vectorlike quarks need to be within the mass range of 2 to 7 times the mass of a standard quark. By studying the process where two muons are produced while a vectorlike quark decays, researchers can now set a minimum mass limit of 1.09 times the mass of a standard quark. Moreover, incorporating vectorlike quarks into the Standard Model through an extension model allows for the creation of certain rare beauty meson decays through a process known as tree-level, which includes the annihilation of two quarks into a vector boson. By analyzing data from the Belle II experiment, we can now set a minimum cross-section threshold of 29 picobarns for these rare decays.

Metric sequence reconstruction is a variation of the classic sequence reconstruction concept, which deals with distance functions. In this context, we examine the distance between permutations using the Hamming method and identify the sequence of Hamming distance functions that allow for the recovery of indices from any given distance measurement. Our analysis reveals that this sequence consists solely of the functions d_3 through d_n for permutations of any length n, which represents an extension to a previous study by Li, Li, and Wang that dealt with distance functions between weighted vectors.

Research on using deep learning for instrument classification has primarily focused on identifying tasks with a large amount of labeled data. To explore the potential of developing efficient models for instrument recognition, this research investigates a few-shot learning approach combined with a hierarchical classification structure. This method allows for the creation of a more compact model that can achieve high accuracy even with limited labeled data. By leveraging the hierarchical organization of instruments, this approach also facilitates the addition of new instruments through self-supervised learning techniques. To test and validate these concepts, a few-shot learning strategy and a hierarchical musical instrument classifier were implemented, and a dataset with over 100 instruments from the Grand Piano to the Harmonica was assembled.

Academic researchers who read research papers often have specific information needs, yet current Information Retrieval systems struggle to efficiently provide the information they're looking for. To make them more effective, we need to create a large dataset that includes both answers and corresponding information sources for questions based on research papers. Creating such a large dataset requires significant human input, which can be costly and time-consuming. In this work, we propose a novel approach to generate high-quality (text, question, answer) datasets by leveraging large language models to create meaningful (question, answer) pairs from existing paragraphs in research papers. Our proposed framework first identifies potential questions within the text, then verifies that the answers provided are accurate with human input. We demonstrate that this efficient approach results in a high-quality dataset that can be used to evaluate and enhance information-seeking question-answering models.

Researchers plan to use pulsar timing arrays to detect gravitational waves from supermassive black hole mergers and other sources. To better analyze data, we need precise models of signals from inspiraling binary systems, especially those with high eccentricity. This study compares various high-accuracy waveform models for eccentric binaries. We compared models that compose Mercury post-Newtonian parameters with models that exclude certain parameters, finding that the former provides a better fit to general relativistic numerical simulations. The performance of these models in analyzing data was also evaluated through simulations, with results indicating that models that omit certain parameters may lead to unanticipated residuals. The composition of parameters affecting model performance was discussed, along with the computational costs associated with each parameter combination.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. We categorize existing research based on the mathematical models employed and discuss their common features and distinctions. Although many models draw heavily from theoretical frameworks, they are currently being developed in response to a real-world epidemic. Consequently, they are being assessed not only by their mathematical coherence and ability to reflect the pandemic's observed behavior, but also by their capacity to reveal key aspects of its transmission dynamics. This research is compiled as an overview of applicable mathematical models, with an emphasis on their relevance to the present COVID-19 situation.

We have analyzed the average and fluctuating behaviors of majorana spin qubits in nitrogen-doped lithium metal. Despite fluctuations in intrinsic properties and chemical environments, we found that majorana fermions exhibit a level of uniformity that is comparable to other systems, as indicated by their spectral density. This level of consistency makes level selection a reliable method for identifying pairs of fermions. Moreover, our study shows that the fermions' level fluctuation follows an Poisson distribution due to level selection, and we found that their average spacing increases over time. These findings support the level spacing as a relevant parameter for qubit operation and demonstrate that fermions with non-interacting behavior can still maintain consistent properties suitable for practical applications.

Acronyms are prevalent in the digital age, yet they pose comprehension challenges due to their frequent occurrence in specialized domains.  Considerable effort has been invested in developing tools to resolve the ambiguity of acronyms, but the name-based terminology often used in these studies makes the work difficult to discover.  To address this issue, we have created a web platform called MadDog, which serves as an all-inclusive resource for identifying and resolving the meaning of acronyms.  This resource not only provides access to existing acronym ambiguity resolution systems, but also offers a collection of corpora containing acronym instances, forward and backward mappings, and annotation tools for resolving the ambiguity of acronyms.  Additionally, MadDog offers a set of preprocessing techniques to automate the annotation of acronyms, and makes the resulting data accessible to the public.

We have theoretically analyzed both recently observed phenomena - spontaneous spinflip recombination of two-spinfermions and recently discovered long-lived state in alkali metal atoms caused by suppression of contact rate between like atoms. Building on these concepts, we explore the possibility of coherent conversion between spinfermions and a molecule through a newly discovered process involving the recombination of two molecules in a spinfermion state, releasing an excess energy in the form of photons. This study focuses on estimating the time it takes for this process to occur and the conditions in which it becomes particularly efficient, namely when there is already an existing molecule in another state, potentially amplifying the conversion between spinfermions and a molecule in a like-spins state and making it possible to achieve a spinfermion-molecule steady state. This phenomenon might prove useful in studying both observed atom-molecule effects and could be applied to a broader class of alkali metal systems.

Our proposed DNA storage management system, called Hierarchical DNA Database (HiDDNA), efficiently handles complex, nested data structures in DNA storage by combining directory and direct mapping techniques. In this hybrid approach, some data blocks are stored within binary directories, while others are mapped to unique DNA addresses and concatenated into longer blocks. A hierarchical directory, made up of smaller, nested binary directories, can then be created to navigate the nested structure of data. HiDDNA updates can be accomplished by modifying DNA blocks or binary directories, with a method provided to convert binary directories into long blocks for consistency. Experimental results demonstrate that HiDDNA significantly reduces the costs of operations on nested data by an average of 5.3 times in comparison to traditional methods.

Topological insulators and other novel quantum states rely heavily on symmetry and the unique behavior of electrons near the Fermi level. Researchers have made significant strides in re-creating these phenomena in 2D and 3D lattices using cold atoms, as well as in structures involving light, spin waves, and photons. This paper delves into the properties of nodal lines in momentum space, focusing on their connection to symmetry and topological invariants. We will examine how certain nodal lines are protected by various symmetries and explore the concept of non-Abelian gauge fields on nodal surfaces. Additionally, we will discuss methods for characterizing these virtual g-force effects and their potential for generating topologically robust light transmission.

A brain tumor affects all age groups and requires prompt diagnosis and treatment due to its ability to impact anyone. Although advanced imaging technology has made it easier to visualize brain tumors, the process of interpreting these images remains a time-consuming and labor-intensive task. Radiologists are typically responsible for identifying tumors and determining their types based on image analysis. To ease this process, researchers have developed image processing techniques that can automatically detect and classify brain tumors. In this research, we present a novel approach called Multi-task Attention Guided Network, which uses a deep learning technique to segment and segment and classify brain tumors in a single process. By applying attention mechanisms to enhance the features extracted from the images, our model achieved exceptional results, outperforming existing methods in terms of accuracy, sensitivity, and other performance metrics.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant interest in image-based inverse problems due to its ability to streamline complex models by bypassing detailed physical and geometric modeling. However, the conventional differentiable renderer based on path tracing faces two major issues that hinder its effectiveness in certain applications. Firstly, it is extremely computationally demanding, and there is a need for a way to accurately estimate shadow intensity without fully simulating light transport. Moreover, existing optimization-based approaches for predicting shadow intensity from observed images are limited by assumptions of static camera positions and scene geometry, and require the creation of multiple images from unknown light sources, which is not always feasible. In this work, we present an efficient and innovative solution that involves jointly optimizing camera pose and scene geometry to derive shadow intensity from images. To achieve this, we introduce a fast and differentiable approach called Shadow Computation via Rendering (SRR) that relies on patch sampling to reduce computational costs. By applying gradient descent to the shadow intensity, our method accurately recovers shadow intensity from images within a few optimization iterations, and is able to handle occluder pose in the presence of camera pose and unknown scene geometry.

A popular video standard known for its high bandwidth and quality is interlaced video, which has a 50% reduction in data compared to progressive video without sacrificing much resolution. However, artifacts can occur in interlaced video due to objects with high-speed movement. Our research proposes a real-time deep learning method to produce high-quality progressive video from interlaced sources. Building upon a recent video super-resolution network, we trained a deep model using an object-based interlaced motion model for optimization. Our system efficiently utilizes GPU for iterative optimization, resulting in high-quality video in real-time. Our method outperforms current video deinterlacing techniques in multiple benchmarks, achieving over 50 frames per second processing speed. A video deinterlacing demo is available at https://youtu.be/046sQ351o4k.

The investigation focuses on the spatial distribution of neutrons in nuclei, specifically in the mean square radius of neutron distribution within RMBM. Notably, RMBM employs non-relativistic equations, utilizing Woods-Saxon potential and the 3$\alpha$ force, whereas RBMR employs the derivation of neutron RMS radius from the square of the wave function for single neutron states. Investigation reveals discrepancies between RMBM results and mean field theory, with some nuclei exhibiting negative neutron RMS radii squares. Furthermore, incorporating spin-orbit force in RMBM yields neutron RMS radii values that closely resemble those obtained from RBMR for both even-even and odd-A nuclei.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for managing flood risks. Hydrologists rely on the shallow water equations, a set of principles that govern river flow, but traditional methods of solving these equations are time-consuming and do not easily accommodate changes in river conditions. This research proposes a novel machine learning model that can quickly predict river flow velocities based on input parameters such as river width, slope, and water viscosity. Unlike conventional dimensionless approaches that rely on idealized conditions, this model is trained on real-world data and can handle the complexities of actual river systems. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in prediction accuracy and processing time, offering a potential tool for real-time flood management.

HDR photography combines multiple photos taken at various exposure levels to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. Current smartphone tri-exposure techniques require the captured images to be well-balanced across three exposure ranges: under-, neutral-, and over-exposed. However, the in-camera automatic exposure selection fails to provide sufficient flexibility. Our research aims to enhance the tri-exposure HDR process by first evaluating the dynamic range of subject images and then using the smartphone's exposure settings to determine the optimal scenes for capturing three balanced photos.

Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible framework. This new class of models has the potential to overcome several limitations of conventional deep learning approaches, such as overfitting, performance degradation when applied to new datasets, and difficulty in understanding the underlying data. Before this emerging field can reach its full potential, researchers must establish a common language and framework to effectively communicate their work. This paper outlines a comprehensive causal graphical representation for machine learning problems, providing a foundation for future work in this field.

Understanding temperature variations within catalytic reactors is crucial for both their efficient design and safe operation. However, currently available temperature measurement techniques have significant limitations in providing real-time, three-dimensional temperature data. In this study, we present a novel approach to obtaining real-time temperature distribution in a fixed bed reactor using rapid MRI, a technique previously unexplored in chemical engineering applications of its kind. We demonstrate the accuracy of MRI temperature measurements against conventional pyrometry measurements and investigate the impact of temperature on MRI image quality, ultimately establishing a temperature range where the method is most effective. We also show that MRI temperature measurements can be improved by adjusting the rate at which the MRI temperature map is acquired. These findings provide a foundation for future implementation of MRI in chemical reactors, offering significant potential for the efficient design and operation of production facilities.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the category of oriented submersions in 2-manifods. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem can be derived from a result by Umehara using these oriented colored broken submersions. Furthermore, it suggests that the Madsen-Weiss theorem can be replaced with the Milnor Mumford conjecture using the same category of map functions.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of various multilevel multigrid methods for cardiac mechanics models. Specifically, we examined how different solvers, including multilevel multigrid, affect the accuracy and speed of solving these models. By incorporating multilevel multigrid as a mult scale preconditioner within a level-set based simulation, we can significantly reduce the time required for simulation. Furthermore, using high performance computing systems allows for faster simulation times, with multilevel multigrid approaching the theoretical optimal time complexity.

The standard scaling for normalized random matrix entries has already been extensively studied. 
However, an examination of the impact of correlation structure on large random matrix ensembles reveals some gaps, as certain high-density scenarios are not fully covered by non-crossing partition theory. 
Our research establishes the limiting spectral distribution for a specific type of symmetric random matrix with positively correlated entries, using a different approach. 
This finding includes examples where the semi-circular law is disrupted and results in the derivation of a new universal formula for spectral distribution. 
This new results can be applied to understand the spectrum of a wide range of random matrix models.

Persuasive multimedia, particularly video, has a powerful impact on targeted audiences through a combination of visual and auditory stimuli. Given its potential, the AI industry is rapidly investing in innovative technologies to produce persuasive video content. However, there is a relative lack of comprehensive research and publications in this domain, making it difficult for new entrants to enter the market. This report focuses specifically on AI-powered persuasive video content creation, examining underlying technical challenges, potential applications, and prominent approaches. Key areas of exploration include text-to-video and video editing models, large-scale video content platforms, and the ethical considerations surrounding AI-generated media. By doing so, this report not only identifies significant challenges ahead but also provides a pathway for future advancements in the field.

Recent studies have uncovered the prevalence of gradient masking in popular defense strategies against adversarial attacks, such as GradNorm. This work scrutinizes the false sense of security GradNorm provides against the parsing-based attack method. We refine the attack algorithm's efficiency and precision, specifically GradNorm in terms of training time and accuracy, respectively. Our experiments demonstrate that just one training iteration with the refined algorithm achieves complete model parsing when using GradNorm, whereas it takes multiple iterations with the original approach. As a consequence, GradNorm's security claims are invalidated by this result.

Recent research has revealed promising properties in microacoustic metagratings when used in the ultrahigh-frequency ultrasound range, specifically above 100 MHz. However, fabricating these structures into three-dimensional shapes with subwavelength dimensions is extremely difficult. As a result, this study presents a novel approach to fabricating complex microacoustic metagrating structures using two-photon lithography. This method allows for the creation of high-precision, three-dimensional structures with features below 10 µm. Specifically, this study demonstrates the use of acoustic multibeam scanning to simultaneously focus multiple high-ultrasound beams onto a fabricated gradient pin-cushion metagrating. High-speed multichannel measurements confirm that the metagrating successfully multibeam-scans acoustic waves in both depth and lateral directions.
