In contrast to this approach, we investigate a global perspective that considers how all training data contributes to the model's predictions. To this end, we develop a rigorous framework for assessing feature importance and conducting adversarial analysis on a Random Forest model using optimal utility theory. Our framework uniquely incorporates both the margin of prediction and a density-based sampling method to ensure a more accurate and efficient analysis. To validate our approach, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation using multiple datasets and a vast number of Random Forest models, demonstrating that, on average, our method correctly identifies the most influential features and facilitates effective adversarial attacks with greater efficiency than state-of-the-art methods.

Minimally invasive surgery has greatly improved overall patient health and overall surgical success rates. Advances in this field have been made possible through innovations in surgical technology, particularly in video enhancement and analysis. One area of focus has been on the development of methods for accurately identifying surgical instruments within the video feed, as this knowledge provides valuable context for what the analyzing system is observing. While previous approaches to image analysis in surgery have shown promise, many of these methods were unable to operate in real-time or relied on enormous data models that required significant processing power. This study explores a range of methods for achieving accurate, real-time instrument identification from raw surgical video, achieving a balance between processing speed and precision that exceeded 95% in many cases.

Current public datasets for re-identifying individuals are limited by the high cost of annotation, which severely hampers their expansion. To address this problem, we propose a novel, large-scale unsupervised re-identification method that utilizes only one image of each individual and requires no prior knowledge of their identity. By developing a public dataset with a vast array of individuals, we provide a platform for evaluating and improving re-identification techniques. Through various approaches that leverage contrastive learning, our research demonstrates the need for region-based techniques to enhance results. These improvements have also had a positive impact on other methodologies, with our best approach achieving a striking 23.6% reduction in error when using the Market-1501 benchmark.

This paper presents an innovative multi-variate measurement GARCH model with a realized threshold, allowing for the examination of time-series data that exhibit varying volatility patterns. We developed a novel threshold model and created an efficient likelihood evaluation method using a specific algorithm. Our framework employs Hidden Markov Model technology to identify distinct volatility periods, and we utilized a Bayesian approach for parameter estimation. Additionally, we evaluated the model's effectiveness in forecasting Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall, demonstrating its superiority over traditional threshold GARCH models. We applied our framework to a two-variate portfolio comprising S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100, and successfully predicted extreme market events during periods of heightened uncertainty.

Determining the parameters of a pulsar's timing model from observed data is a common practice in both research and education. Researchers typically employ the least squares method for this purpose. However, an unexpected finding emerged when comparing the robust regression method to the least squares approach. The most satisfactory result from the robust method corresponds to a modified version of the timing model that includes additional terms. These extra terms are associated with phenomena such as the long-term frequency acceleration and the Sagnelli effect in gravity, which are widely regarded as anomalies in the data.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory.

The evolution of low-mass pre-main sequence stars is determined by their mass, which is in turn affected by the accretion rate. To investigate this relationship, researchers need to account for the scatter in data, as the distribution of accretion rates among young stars is not uniform. Previous studies have suggested that active accretion processes could contribute to this scatter, but this has not been thoroughly explored. This study aims to assess the impact of activity and short-term variability on the data, using a uniform analysis method to calculate the mass, age, and accretion rate of a sample of stars. This study focuses on the Trappist-1 and Pleiades clusters, specifically examining the XX Cha and XX Canum Venaticorum, and finds that XX Cha exhibits a high degree of mass-dependent variability in its accretion rate, which could have significant implications for the interpretation of accretion data.

This study explores how uncertainty about chance influencing job success and earnings impacts redistribution policies in a diverse group of people. We gather responses from a group of participants, who consider various scenarios in which good luck can affect worker productivity, and whose data reveals that: (i) learning that luck has a greater share of responsibility in earnings can increase support for redistribution but also (i) decrease the perceived importance of unequal opportunities and (i) decrease the impact of learning that luck matters on the desire for more aggressive redistribution policies. We also examine how the desire for more equal chances influences the impact of support for redistribution in various groups of people.

Removing a subspace from a partial flag results in another partial flag consisting of fewer components. This action induces a mapping $\pi: X \to X'$ between corresponding flag varieties, which essentially discards information about certain components of a given flag. As a consequence, the quantum K-theory kernel $K_{q}(\pi)$ of this map carries a specific structural property that can be leveraged to induce a similar structural feature within the Okounkov semiring $K_{q}(X')$ of the target flag variety $X'$.

On the one hand, we establish that $K_{q}(\pi)$ possesses a compact module-like structure over $K_{q}(X')$. On the other hand, recent breakthrough by Okounkov and Rubinstein-Zhghaev has demonstrated that $K_{q}(\pi)$ is isomorphic to a direct sum of delayed quantum $K$-theories associated with another partial flag variety $X''$, which can be constructed from $X'$ and $X$ by combining certain indices.

In this work, we extend this result to a more general setting by proving a similar decomposition holds for a direct summand of the quantum $K$-theoretic stable bundle map $\sigma_{*}: K(X) \to K(Y)$ between any two smooth varieties $X$ and $Y$. The development of data-driven machine learning applications is hindered by poor quality training datasets, a problem exacerbated by the complex relationship between datasets and model performance. This issue makes identifying and rectifying data defects challenging. This research paper explores the use of Shapley values from the machine learning explanation framework to debug data. We present an initial approach to this problem and a prototype that integrates this explanatory tool with a comprehensive machine learning pipeline. This prototype is capable of running selected machine learning explanation algorithms and can leverage Shapley values to assess the importance of individual training samples and potential data issues. This research presents our findings and results from a case study that illustrates the effectiveness of our data debugging method.

We investigated the connection between radio and X-ray emissions in 1111 galaxy clusters from the MAVERIC Survey using deep, high-resolution observations. A novel method was used to determine the dynamical state of each cluster by analyzing the velocity dispersion of stars. We established a relationship between dynamic and photometric properties, identifying a specific pattern that separates active from inactive clusters. A new model combining a power-law and an exponential function accurately describes this data. We identified three distinct populations: collisionless core candidates, X-ray sources, and the majority of radio-emitting clusters. We distinguished between magnetized and unmagnetized clusters by analyzing the B-field of their radio emissions. We discovered a specific group of galaxy clusters with both radio and X-ray emissions that are dynamically active, potentially linked to the dynamic behavior of the clusters. We propose that the magnetic fields of these clusters are linked to their radio emissions, and that the dynamic nature of some clusters may influence the relationship between their X-ray and radio emissions. This study paves the way for a comprehensive investigation of the connection between magnetic fields and dynamic phenomena in galaxy clusters.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks can be more effectively modeled as hypergraphs rather than graphs, but the necessary data is often available only as projected graphs. In this study, we formulate a high-dimensional hypergraph reconstruction problem and develop a supervised learning approach to solve it. Our proposed method combines graph embedding techniques with a novel hypergraph recovery algorithm. Evaluations on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that our algorithm significantly outperforms baseline methods in various link prediction and classification tasks. Furthermore, we apply it successfully to identify protein functional groups.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited due to the difficulty in defining it and its inability to capture the entire space around the microcavity.

The scattering of coherent light from heated alkali metals in a range of 400-600 Kelvin is examined in detail, and atomic fluorescence and transmitted light characteristics are measured using different alkali metal samples. A theoretical model is developed to explain the phenomena observed, and it demonstrates that a thermal rate equation framework can accurately describe even complex behaviors in both single and multi-level systems across various transitions and wavelength combinations. The model predicts light characteristics in line with those seen in experiments, and it also allows for a clear understanding of the influence of temperature on fluorescence and transmitted light dynamics. Notably, it is demonstrated that in some cases, the statistical properties of light in transmission are heavily affected by temperature, and that the phenomenon of super-Poissonian light in transmission can arise due to a combination of constructive and destructive interference within the system. Furthermore, the research provides valuable insights into the emergence of entanglement between alkali metals in a heated ensemble.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing practical applications of learning models for multiple interacting entities. Nevertheless, offline data often lacks sufficient diversity in the quality of experiences that different agents have. Simply averaging the value function estimates from policy evaluation methods can lead to inaccurate results. In response, we introduce a novel approach called Quality-Aware (QuA) that aims to select more valuable trajectories for both single agents and systems of interacting agents. The approach involves re-weighting transition probabilities to give greater importance to high-quality trajectories, and then estimating a modified reward function that can be learned by standard policy evaluation techniques from these trajectories. The results from our experiments show that the QuA method outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches in the offline single-agent setting and has significant potential for improvement in applications involving multiple interacting agents.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they are limited by local convergence and computationally demanding processes. This study proposes utilizing artificial intelligence to accelerate and enhance image registration, specifically for modern treatments employing megavoltage imaging. Although research into using artificial intelligence for registration exists, image-based convolutional neural network methods have been primarily applied to modality-specific imaging. This study presents a pioneering approach for image registration utilizing a convolutional neural network, leveraging the advanced capabilities of artificial intelligence. We employed a convolutional neural network to learn an optimal mapping between a moving image and a fixed reference image, resulting in a deformation field that aligns the images. This approach was tested on 2D CT images and expanded to include 3D CBCT and CT images. By training a convolutional neural network on a large dataset, we achieved efficient and optimal image registration, outperforming conventional algorithms such as mutual information registration. This approach demonstrated significant improvements in registration accuracy and efficiency, with reduced execution times and higher Dice similarity coefficients.

In 1927, Einstein used the solubility of the Schrödinger equation for localized particles to argue against the nonlocality inherent in the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics. However, the nonlocality of the Copenhagen interpretation was later confirmed by Bell's theorem. To resolve this apparent contradiction, Einstein proposed a thought experiment that would have demonstrated the existence of macroscopic superpositions. We reexamine his thought experiment and find that the outcome can be fully explained by local hidden variables, indicating that the nonlocal effects of quantum mechanics can also manifest in single-particle systems. We further show that the phenomenon of single-particle steering, where the wave function of a spatially separated part of a system is "steered" by a measurement on the other part, gives rise to a violation of Bell's inequality.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning into Internet of Vehicles systems has significantly improved their functionality and efficiency. However, enhancing these systems' security and privacy has become an ongoing challenge. This paper introduces a novel approach called Federated Learning, which allows multiple entities to collaboratively train machine learning models without sharing sensitive data. To overcome the limitations of traditional Federated Learning, researchers are exploring the use of Blockchain technology to create a secure and transparent framework. This review examines existing research on Federated Learning models for Internet of Vehicles, highlighting their vulnerabilities and security concerns. It also explores potential solutions through a blockchain-enabled Federated Learning framework and identifies areas for future development in this rapidly evolving field.

V392 Persei is an active binary system that experienced a surprising event in November 2018, when it suddenly emitted an intense burst of \gamma-rays and X-rays about 10 orders of magnitude brighter than its normal outbursts.  V392 Persei is well-known and extensively researched, with multiple observational indicators pointing to its classification as a dwarf nova, specifically a system undergoing a rare and explosive event known as an IKN.  Before the outburst, astronomers had already detected V392 Persei among a group of systems predicted to undergo such events based on their accretion disk instability timescales.  V392 Persei is unusual in that its \gamma-ray activity, which began about a month after typical novae, lasted for over 10 months, with the \gamma-ray emission gradually decreasing over time.  V392 Persei is predicted to be one of the systems most likely to undergo a \gamma-ray bright event in the coming years.  However, its actual classification is still being debated, with some researchers suggesting it was an extremely rare and previously unobserved type of eruption, which they call an \xi-class outburst.

In quantum computing, incorporating more than two qubits into a single gate provides significant advantages over using two-qubit gates, resulting in performance improvements. However, incorporating error correction into the computation diminishes these benefits. We investigated substitulating Cryan-Laflamme-Pzterek (CLP) two-qubit gates with their multi-qubit extensions within the toric code's framework, a widely used baseline. We observed that while an increase in qubits engaged during a single gate caused a modest increase in susceptibility to noise, it consistently remained below the system's threshold using two-qubit multi-qubit error prevention. In contrast, using unrelated two-qubit gates resulted in significantly higher susceptibility to noise, a considerable increase above using their multi-qubit equivalents. These findings suggest that incorporating larger quantum gates into fault-tolerant computing systems could yield substantial performance gains.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding method leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. The mobile terminal channel is modeled as a sum of independent narrowband signals, with each component associated with a specific GMM component. By matching these GMM components to the codebook entries, the mobile terminal identifies the most significant mixture components, selects the corresponding codebook entries, and encerts feedback using rate-limited quantization, achieving rate efficiency gains from both codebook size reduction and quantization.

A new phenomenon of robust non-equilibrium surface currents in a 3D magnetic torus has been identified, stemming from unique nonequilibrium Bloch oscillations of a single particle. This effect is found in systems with 3D offset Hamiltonians and is notably insensitive to the structure of a lattice. As a consequence, large cross-sectional Hall currents in 2D slices through such systems can persist even when disorder is present, and these currents can be toggled between two states by altering the orientation of a sample.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at infinity without a source, we've derived a new upper limit on the Bondi mass decay rate in relation to the total radiated energy flux. A possible derivation from general relativity is being explored for this empirical bound.

We examine the potential gravitational wave background from massive stars in nuclear star clusters, specifically focusing on pairs of merging black holes and black hole mergers involving remnant stars in quasars. Our analysis shows that under certain conditions, these events could create a distinct, trackable gravitational wave background that could be detected by future observatories like LISA and Einstein Telescope. However, their formation requires extremely rare occurrences, making their contribution to the GWB negligible. Instead, a more probable scenario arises from star formation in supermassive black hole power-law tails, which would contribute minimally to the GWB but significantly to the GWB in distinct GW events, particularly in mergers of supermassive black holes.

The primary goal of the Gravitational Wave high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) is to detect and localize Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) that arise from the merger of compact binary objects, which also helps localize the subsequent production of gravitational waves by particles emitted by said objects or nucleosynthesis. To verify the GRB localization performance of the GECAM, we created a portable GRB simulator that can replicate the response of GECAM's onboard Wide Field Detectors (WFDs) to both simulated and real GRBs. This simulator was built using a personal computer and can precisely duplicate the WFD's energy spectrum, temporal evolution, and various triggering patterns. As an alternative to traditional methods of GRB positioning, such as calculating the equivalent energy of each WFD, we developed a more accurate method of GRB localization by training a Deep Neural Network (DNN) to analyze the raw data from WFDs. This approach was first used to locate two highly detailed simulations of GRBs, resulting in 90% confidence levels of 2.24 arcmin and 4.56 arcmin, which are comparable to the 100% confidence levels of 2.56 arcmin and 4.56 arcmin for respectively Grand Design I and II, which are also the official standards set by the China National Space Administration (CNSA). This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by Block-Kr\"{u}sperger. We focus on determining the operator norms of the semigroup of composition operators on BMOA_p as well as its analogue VMOA_p, given the standard assumptions on the semigroup's phi functions. In addition, this article explores the relationship between the operator norms of the semigroup of composition operators on BMOA_p and VMOA_p, revealing that they share a comparable $\Phi$ function. We also discuss the long-standing conjecture by Zhu regarding the behavior of the operator norms of the semigroup of composition operators on H^p when the semigroup is generated by the infinitesimal generator containing the operator $\varphi(z)\overline{z'}$. We also examine the operator bounds of the semigroup of integral operators on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p, given the kernel function $K$ satisfying certain conditions.

Humanity's vast unknowns, fueled by the Disproportion Between Scientific Productivity and Knowledge Amount, have a strong basis in Einstein's words. A notable gap exists between scientific productivity and the amount of knowledge, which has been disproportionately balanced. This imbalance, which grows at an exponential rate, can be classified into four categories: redundancy, ineffectiveness, inaccessibility, and disorganization. Redundancy arises from conflicting information, necessitating a means to discern reliable data. Ineffectiveness stems from the human brain's inability to process excessive details, requiring concise and concise information presentation. Inaccessibility results from the exclusion of specialized knowledge, requiring a method to integrate diverse knowledge systems. Disorganization arises from the lack of a unified theoretical framework, requiring a means to integrate disparate information. A comparative analysis of the human brain and the distribution of scientific data reveals that a logarithmic distribution, which represents the majority of scientific information, differs from the normal distribution, which represents the majority of human knowledge. This finding has significant implications for a new approach to addressing this proportionate discrepancy, which involves a shift in perspective, a unifying theoretical framework, a mapping system, and a concise language.

In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use frequency-based transmission. To mitigate this threat, we investigate a security-enhancing technique in which a single relay transmits data using multiple relayed sub-channels. We focus on a scenario in which a malicious receiver knows the communication channels but has limited knowledge of the relay's secrecy code. By optimizing this secrecy code, we can maximize the system's security even when the malicious receiver's knowledge of the channels is not perfect. This code-optimization problem is resolved using a sequence of lower-bound approximation methods. Physical layer security gains achieved through this investigation are illustrated with numerical examples.

Two-dimensional systems with robust edge currents due to large Chern numbers offer a wealth of chiral modes at each energy level and along each edge.  
By strategically positioning quantum emitters in the waveguide, we can couple them to multiple modes, resulting in interactions that scale as the square of the photon coupling rate, which can be quite substantial near edges.  
We identify an effective model that captures these emitter-EM field interactions, which comprises two-body terms representing the transport of photons carried by multiple channels, and strongly intensity-dependent two-body terms that arise from Emitters' interactions.  
In addition, we find that emitters can exhibit non-trivial topological properties, with their local environments characterized by non-zero winding numbers, leading to the emergence of topologically protected states, including chiral photons with two quantized values of momentum, all within a planar setup.

You won to the paper's abstract which delivers a novel predictive control framework for safety-aware connected automated vehicles (CAVs) regulated by traffic signals. An optimization model was developed that takes into account external forces and predicts CAV dynamics over a specific time period at an intersection where multiple lanes meet. The model includes a PDE-based two-phase traffic model which accounts for CAVs and traffic jams. By applying the prediction, the cost function of an optimal control problem is informed, allowing the intersection clearance of CAVs to be prioritized. A data-driven predictive control strategy was proposed that utilizes a stochastic CAV dynamical model and ensures safety by minimizing the probability of collisions. Finally, a method was described for determining optimal acceleration commands that minimize expected collision probabilities.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to evaluate virtual agents, yet their underlying systems have limited speed and use unrealistic data. We present TextWorldExpress, an enhanced text-based game platform with ten times greater speed, realistic imagery, and a vast, diverse database. TextWorldExpress offers a comprehensive and rapidly processed dataset of 100 virtual agents' performance across numerous text-based games.

Deep learning models, specifically Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks.  However, their significant computational and memory requirements hinder their deployment on energy-constrained devices for complex applications like video recognition.  This problem is exacerbated by the inefficiency of conventional RNN implementations that disregard the unique properties of LSTM structures for optimizing calculations and memory usage.  In this study, we present an algorithm and system co-design that enables accurate and energy-efficient LSTM computations and optimizations, particularly for video recognition on FPGAs.  Our approach integrates a customized computation and memory architecture with a data compression algorithm based on hierarchical tensor decomposition, resulting in substantial improvements in peak memory usage and energy consumption compared to conventional methods.  By applying this approach to video recognition using an LSTM-based hardware accelerator, we observe up to 2.17x and 3.13x improvements in memory consumption and energy consumption, respectively, while achieving comparable accuracy to state-of-the-methods on the TSVd dataset.

Significant advancements in NLP have been made possible by neural networks, particularly in scenarios where vast amounts of labeled data are available. However, NLP tasks that are reliant on domain-specific data often struggle due to small datasets, which are typically insufficient to achieve high levels of accuracy. As a result, data augmentation techniques have been extensively investigated to enhance limited datasets by artificially increasing their size through various methods. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of data augmentation techniques for improving limited datasets in NLP, with an emphasis on their underlying principles, practical implementations, and empirical results. NLP's sensitivity to 标签 (tags) makes data augmentation a particularly useful tool for addressing scenarios where large volumes of labeled data are not readily accessible.

The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is best articulated through its implication of the existence of a particle that is charged but has no mass. A key indicator of the validity of this conjecture lies in the presence of a certain type of state within the theory, specifically a convexly charged state that has the lowest possible mass. This work aims to provide a clearer and more rigorous mathematical definition of charge convexity, as well as a set of criteria to check for it. The study then provides several examples of definitions of charge convexity and confirms the presence of a certain type of state in the large N limit of the $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory, confirming a prediction made by the Weak Gravity Conjecture. The work also explores the convexity of the potential of the axion monodromy inflation and the feasibility of checking charge convexity in the context of the Swampland's Covariant Swampland Conjecture.

To stabilize the estimation of ground and excited states on a quantum computer, we modify the quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to utilize the model space. This model-space QITE method can efficiently find excited states of complex systems that interact in multiple states. By applying a unitary operator in the model space to simulate the progression of imaginary time, the algorithm converges rapidly to target states when starting from an orthogonal initial state. We've developed an innovative algorithm for model-space QITE with proof of convergence, and demonstrated that it outperforms the standard orthogonal QITE. The model-space QITE achieves a significant reduction in evolution steps by leveraging the model unitary operator, and targets both states within the model space that share the highest overlap with the initial state. By decomposing the systems' Hamiltonian into real and imaginary components, the model-space QITE can be executed using only two circuit executions per evolution step, allowing for the estimation of Re and Im components of the model unitary operator to obtain the desired results. The model-space QITE was also shown to efficiently calculate excited states of the spin-boson system and atomic Rydberg systems.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic, we introduce a class of rings, denoted as $\mathcal{I}$, which possess a property where the tight Hilbert polynomial of the ring remains consistent across the characteristic two through five. It is demonstrated that being $F$-rational in nature is an equivalent condition to being located within the category of rings $\mathcal{I}$, including those defined by a specific singularity exponent and tight Hilbert polynomial. For instance, being $F$-rational is equivalent to having a finite $F$-signature if and only if the ring's Krull dimension is less than or equal to four. Additionally, being $F$-rational is equivalent to having a positive tight Hilbert polynomial of degree equal to the ring's Krull dimension if and only if the ring's Krull dimension is less than or equal to three.

The growth of decentralized and low-emission electricity generation is being hindered by technical grid stability issues. To address this challenge, ancillary services are crucial for ensuring grid reliability and are increasingly being obtained through dynamic market mechanisms. However, existing studies on market analysis often fail to consider the grid's broader impact and are limited to very small participant groups. In contrast, our research focuses on a more comprehensive model that examines the importance of ancillary services in dynamic markets and develops a dynamic endogenous model that analyzes the impact of market activity on a small number of large participants. Our developed model also allows us to explore the efficiency of market designs and the potential role of policy in guiding large participants to invest in low-emission generation. We found that the ancillary services market can be beneficial and that investing in low-emission generation can be profitable, but this outcome is not guaranteed and depends on market conditions. Therefore, the potential role of policy in guiding large participants to make this investment is significant.

Wu and Xiao's research, from 2017, indicates the presence of the Schinzel property in the iterates of certain polynomial compositions. We extend this work by establishing a connection between the prime factorization complexity that remains invariant in iterated primes and that which is prime in specialized values. This in turn enables us to establish the Schinzel property for a broader class of polynomials through the application of results obtained by Fried in 1983.

This paper presents a matrix element level Monte Carlo simulation for producing a Higgs boson pair through a non-resonant process at the Large Hadron Collider, highlighting a new method for accurately handling final state particles. By utilizing an exact calculation of a four-body decay, one can more precisely simulate the interactions and improve the signal to background ratio for certain detection methods. To demonstrate this approach, we applied it to a specific process involving the production of a Higgs boson pair through gluon fusion and the detection of two of the four final decay products, specifically quark-antiquark pairs from the Higgs boson decay into a bottom quark pair and vector bosons from the other decay. We found that this method significantly increases the signal to background ratio in this process compared to the standard method where the Wiggs decay into bottom quark pairs.

We leverage an overlooked potential in precision measurements of the standard process $e^+e^-\to Zh$ to probe a wide range of physics beyond the Standard Model linked to extended scalar sectors. By precisely analyzing this process and the associated Standard Model Higgs production and decay to photons, we establish stringent limits on various BHSS models including the Complex Two-Doublet Model (CTDM), Two-Higgs Doublet Model (2HDM), and Multi-Doublet Model (MDM). The future Super Flavor Factory (SFF) will significantly enhance our sensitivity to these theories, allowing for precision tests up to energy levels of 10 times the electroweak scale.

Saturn's polar atmosphere is divided into two opposing seasonal extremes. During Saturn's northern summer, a prominent warm spot appears in the UV images of the planet, while the rest of the season is marked by the gradual development of a polar night vortex. Researchers used the Juno spacecraft to measure the temperature variations within the planet's upper atmosphere as it passed through Saturn's north pole, providing a comprehensive view of the region. Analysis of the temperature data revealed the characteristics of the polar night vortex, which was still influenced by the previously active warm spot, located at approximately 80 km above the planet's cloud tops. A distinct temperature anomaly within the stratosphere, which was isolated from the dynamic mesosphere below, provided evidence of the vortex's existence. The axis of the vortex was tilted towards the approaching equator, while the part of the atmosphere beyond 2 bar above the 88°N latitude circle was isolated from the surrounding mid-latitudes. A large warm spot, which was located beyond the 85°N latitude circle, was observed 1.5 bar wide and 2 bar deep. Additionally, a narrow, 1-bar long, 60° wide warm jet stream was found at the edge of the polar warm spot, reinforcing the stratospheric "hexagon" that has been observed from Earth and space for decades. We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

The behavior of V$_2$O$_3$ ultrathin films is intriguing due to their metal-insulator transition, which differs from their bulk properties and can be altered at specific critical thicknesses. A recent study investigated the insulating properties of a 24-unit-cell-thick V$_2$O$_3$ film grown on sapphire, and discovered that its electronic structure is heavily influenced by surface termination layers. By comparing theoretical models of different surface terminations with experimental angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy data, the study revealed that only one particular surface layer configuration matches the observed electronic behavior. Furthermore, it was found that this particular surface layer exhibits unique electron correlation effects, and that adding electron count can lead to a shift in the electron behavior. This study highlights the importance of controlling surface layer configuration in determining the electronic properties of V$_2$O$_3$ ultrathin films.

Our study provides new insights into the one-dimensional interaction of two quantum double dark-soliton pairs, based on a precise expression of the model's thermodynamic properties. By applying a semi-classical method, we obtain a detailed understanding of how certain particle densities and a specific spin correlation behave as the system transitions from a finite to an infinitely large scale. This approach yields a more accurate approximation than previous methods and demonstrates a near-exact match with direct numerical simulations, even for systems of moderate size. Furthermore, it reveals a subtle, log-periodic oscillation in the residual Bose-Einstein condensation fraction, which may have significant implications for similar systems found in nature.

We create a linearisation functor for full linearisation that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Our analysis includes an examination of its properties and various applications. Additionally, we define the categories of k-fold vector bundles and graded bundles of degree k, establish a full linearisation functor from graded bundles of degree k to vector bundles of degree k, and explore its properties. Furthermore, we discuss semi-linearisation functors.

This informal note begins by illustrating some technical concepts, including the re-normalization of measures on orbital integrals from the works of Langlands and Kottwitz, to prepare for the re-normalization program outlined in the associated paper.

The interaction between light and matter is utilized in various spectroscopic techniques to extract information about a system's structure. Techniques like x-ray crystallography provide detailed atomic and molecular structure data, but combining these approaches could lead to a more comprehensive understanding of light-matter interactions. A new method, known as phase retrieval spectroscopy, has been developed to automatically determine the complex scattering factors of any system from reflected intensity patterns. Utilizing x-ray free-electron lasers and the resulting coherent x-ray light, this technique was demonstrated to accurately reconstruct nuclear arrangements in complex materials such as CaCu_3Ti_4O_12, NaFe_2(OH)_6, and Si, even when subtle features like nuclear phase distortions or bond angles are present. Phase retrieval spectroscopy has the potential to be a powerful tool with broad applications in understanding nuclear and electron structures in various scientific fields.

By linking quantum error correction circuits to disordered Ising spin models, a new method has been developed to identify and analyze difficult regions in the circuit that cause probability distributions to mix slowly. This approach provides a practical way to determine the minimum circuit depth required to verify the operation of quantum operations and error corrections on the SZZ code when various physical errors are applied. Using this method, the feasible operating point of this code is established by testing circuit connectivity on a second-order tensor network and confirming its shape through simulations. Additionally, this relationship can be applied to evaluate the performance of other topological quantum computing systems.

Recent theoretical predictions have identified topological phase transitions and a large energy gap in the tellurene monolayer, which is a square-shaped structure. However, its stability in isolation is questionable. We propose a single-atom-thick Te layer with bond-lengths that match first-principles calculations for isolated and substrate-supported tellurene. We find that in a flattened structure, both intrinsic and doped topological properties are preserved in supported tellurene, offering the potential for efficient 2D topological insulators.

We devise a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures that intersect at right angles. This method employs traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model the fractures, which results in a high-dimensional discretization of the matrix domain and a reduced one-dimensional discretization of the fractures. This approach avoids the issues of locking and poor convergence rates that arise from the dimensional crossover phenomenon. Our scheme effectively captures the appropriate $O(h)$ and $O(H)$ convergence rates for the numerical errors, where $h$ and $H$ denote the respective local mesh sizes for the matrix and fractures. This method is also applicable to more complex scenarios involving sources/sinks and time-dependent problems. Furthermore, our research provides clear visual illustrations of the method's efficacy.

A comprehensive examination of a spin-triplet superconducting device, which involves a spiral magnetic arrangement, is conducted. The underlying metal exhibits unique magnetic characteristics, while adjacent insulating and superconducting layers are analyzed. A combination of these materials results in distinct magnetic and superconducting phenomena, including a tilt in magnetization and spin-triplet pairing with notable flat components. Notably, a spin-triplet device displays significantly higher resistance in contrast to its triplet-majority counterpart during transitions between superconducting and normal states. Through a metal's thickness examination, an abrupt resistance drop in specific configurations is observed. Furthermore, a superconducting critical temperature enhancement in certain orientations is evident when comparing to conventional single-triplet devices.

Hypothesis testing is a crucial aspect of scientific inquiry, yet it is often viewed unfavorably due to its association with the p-value. In contrast, Bayes factors are underutilized for their potential to thoroughly assess both proposed and alternative theories. This paper aims to fill a significant knowledge gap by offering a comprehensive review of the literature on Bayes factors for hypothesis evaluation. Due to the existing disparity in research on this topic, we adopted an iterative process involving visualizations and author feedback to structure the vast amount of literature. Moreover, we propose a proposal-testing framework and provide accompanying code to facilitate the analysis. Due to the inherent uncertainty in estimating Bayes factors, particularly with large sample sizes, our review emphasizes the need to consider multiple prior distributions. We also discuss potential strategies to enhance the consistency and reliability of Bayes factors in such situations.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "unfortunately" facilitate the interpretation of text by conveying relationships between sentences. To enhance this capability for news documents, we created a discourse indicator classification system that identifies whether these indicators signify positive or negative information within articles. This system was developed using a dataset consisting of 10,000 articles from which 1,000 were used to train the system and another 1,000 served as a benchmark. Our model was trained using a combination of linguistic features and information extracted from the content of the sentences, then evaluated against a dataset where discourse indicators were manually annotated. The results showed our approach can accurately classify these indicators, enabling the downstream application of information enrichment tools that can pinpoint where in articles specific information is located.

We investigated the properties of a collection of approximately 10 million diamond nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers in a microwave resonator, spanning a wide temperature range from 77K to 550K.  Our study included measurements of the spin coherence time and line widths under various temperatures.  We found that at high temperatures above 200K, the NV zero-phonon line begins to broaden due to the influence of the Debye-Waller factor.  Our data was fitted using a widely used rate equation model, and the extracted parameters were in line with published results.  Notably, our parameters for the quadrupolar splitting and the quadrupole coupling constant were previously unreported in the literature for this specific crystal orientation.

The backpropagation algorithm, though effective for training neural networks, has a significant drawback: it mandates the sharing of weights. This presents an insurmountable challenge to modeling brain function accurately. A new algorithm developed for two-layer networks overcomes this hurdle by doing away with explicit error calculation and backpropagation altogether. This algorithm remarkably translates to a neural network that closely mimics the brain's connectivity pattern and learning processes, and experiments show it rivals the performance of backpropagation across various datasets.

Using field-theoretic methods, researchers investigated a spin model on the triangular lattice, where $SU(3)$ spins interact via a long-range exchange interaction on the three-colouring triangular honeycomb grid. The analysis revealed the presence of two distinct spiral magnetic phases, with spins twisting in $(1,1,-2)$ patterns along the lattice axes. At zero density, this interaction is equivalent to the standard $SU(3)$ Heisenberg model. The study also compared its model to a two-dimensional dimerized $SU(3)$ Hubbard model, where a strong dimerization arises from virtual hopping processes. The research found that a repulsive Hubbard interaction leads to a spiral order described by the spin model's $(1,1,-2)$ state.

A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for well-behaved central potentials. The method employs a flexible B-spline basis in combination with a numerical evaluation of the exchange potential, allowing for precise determination of HF eigenvalues and occupied orbitals. By increasing the basis set, the method can smoothly transform the description of atomic systems from quantum HF eigenstates to an electron gas model with zero density. Notably, we demonstrate that the method converges to the exact random-phase approximation even with finite electron densities, achieving this result with just a moderate expansion of the basis set.

The distinction between orderly and chaotic behavior within complex networks of interdependent oscillators corresponds to varying functional states found in numerous intricate systems, including those seen in electronic circuits, neural activity, and the dynamic relationships between species in ecology. Researchers have recently discovered that explosive transitions between stable and chaotic states can occur in interconnected systems of interdependent limit cycle oscillators, but this requirement for pre-existing stable states limits its applicability. Our study develops an analytical framework to identify whether abrupt transitions will happen in complex, multi-layered networks of coupled oscillators that interact with each other through various topologies, whether simple or chaotic, within two interconnected systems to highly heterogeneous nodes. Our analysis reveals that explosive transitions will occur when the distribution of connections among network users follows a specific pattern, known as the area under the cumulative cumulative distribution function (CCDF) of the connection distribution, which must be less than one. Our simulations confirm that this criterion holds true across a broad range of complex networks, and we propose that it can serve as a guiding principle for predicting and controlling the explosive transitions that occur within complex systems.

We investigate a widely used matrix factorization approach for solving large-scale, rank-constrained optimization problems. Assuming a key condition holds, we demonstrate that a more efficient loss function minimum can be achieved by the standard matrix factorization method compared to the minimum of the underlying constrained problem. This indicates that the matrix factorization method has a challenging landscape that contains additional spurious minima. To better understand this, we analyze the global structure of the loss landscape for a specific class of problems that exhibit this behavior. For a more in-depth examination, we focus on identifying all critical points in the neighborhood of a particular solution. Our research has a general nature and provides a template for studying the complex landscape of matrix factorization methods. It also reveals that a condition we used has a connection to the property of geodesic convexity, thus highlighting the importance of considering landscape properties that are relevant to optimization algorithms in practice.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a certain distance criteria, specifically a distance-two-based condition.  In the context of a bipartite graph, a strong edge coloring condition is met if all edges of a certain graph receive different colors, then the strong edge chromatic number of that graph is the minimum number of colors needed to achieve this condition.  Currently, the edge chromatic number of a cubic bipartite graph is proven to be no more than its maximum degree, but the same is not known about the strong edge chromatic number of such graphs.  We have identified a counterexample to the conjecture that the strong edge chromatic number of any cubic bipartite graph is no more than its maximum squared, by presenting a specific quadrangulated graph that requires more colors than this threshold.

Let $q$ be an integer greater than one, and let $\chi$ denote a Dirichlet character associated with $q$. The article discusses the orthogonality properties of Dirichlet $L$-functions, specifically examining the sum $\sum_{\chi\ (\mathrm{mod}\ q)} L(\chi, s)$. We will now look at some novel identities of Dirichlet $L$-functions and discuss their proof.

Extending the Standard Model to include an unstable particle with an extremely high mass is a possible theory. This model involves two scalar fields that spontaneously create an unstable maximum, allowing for an arbitrary particle mass. However, this situation would have been resolved early in the universe's history due to thermal fluctuations. A possible resolution to this problem is if the model includes an effective negative curvature which restricts the universe to a small volume until it reaches T~10^10 K. This model also includes predictions for the production of defects and particles in extremely high energies.

Our experiments examined how the geometric structure of force-free rigid swimmers interacts with different fluid properties, specifically focusing on how swimming speed and orientation are affected by viscosity. By comparing swimmers with opposite chirality and different front-back symmetry, we investigated their swimming speeds in Newtonian fluids and then extended these studies to non-Newtonian power law fluids. The data showed that while the impact of viscoelasticity on swimming speed in complex fluids is substantial, how it influences swimming in purely viscous fluids is minimal, with visible effects only in swimmers with intricate geometric designs, or those with different front and back shapes. Furthermore, we found that the relationship between swimming speed and viscosity varies depending on both the swimmer's geometry and the viscoelastic properties of the surrounding fluid, with one notable outcome being that swimming in the same direction can be slower than swimming in the opposite direction in certain viscoelastic environments.

We employ co-evolutionary genetic algorithms to model the behavior of a large number of players in a Cournot market and demonstrate their effectiveness in predicting the Nash equilibrium. Specifically, we develop a method to translate the strategies produced by the algorithm into payoffs and quantities that accurately reflect the predicted Nash equilibrium. We then compare our results with those of a standard genetic algorithm, which randomly generates strategies, in an attempt to establish the Nash equilibrium. It is found that our method significantly improves accuracy, particularly in markets with a limited number of participants.

The growth of ontologies has significantly contributed to various domains, particularly in improving information retrieval from the web. One viable strategy to keep them current and comprehensive is identifying and incorporating newly mentioned entities in academic papers or other text. To achieve this, we've developed a 2-stage framework to identify novel entities from base entities. In the first stage, we employ a Context-Word Representation (CWR) model to extract all potential entities from text. Following that, we classify the entities as new or existing ones based on a given set of base entities, using a support vector machine (SVM) in the second stage. Experimental results on two datasets, including a custom one, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Furthermore, we've shown its practical application in enhancing the Fishbase ontology.

The proposed Ising-doped voter model, an hybrid model with elements from the Ising and voter models, was developed to illustrate how systems out of equilibrium reach stable states, specifically on large networks. While previous studies focused on its equational states on large networks, this analysis also examined its typical dynamics on small networks using simulation and theoretical modeling. Findings revealed that at high-temperature conditions, the system reached a temperature-dependent state on large networks within the temperature intervals below a specific threshold through either sudden or gradual transitions. At low-temperature conditions, the system reached a persistent state by absorbing a small portion of the network's magnetization, thus isolating a small group within the population.

Understanding how viruses spread through the air isCrucial in comprehending pandemic dynamics and developing effective mitigation strategies. Weather conditions significantly impact the duration viruses remain suspended in the air, yet our current knowledge of this phenomenon varies across different climates. To better grasp the global spread of these pathogens, it is essential to investigate how atmospheric conditions affect their persistence in the air under different weather scenarios. In this research, we develop and apply a model to analyze the physical processes involved in the spread of respiratory viruses through the air under different atmospheric conditions. Our findings indicate that increased temperature and humidity facilitate viral settling, while low relative humidity contributes to longer-lasting viruses in the air. Additionally, our study reveals that viruses can travel considerable distances through the air, even small droplets can remain suspended for an extended period, affecting communities beyond initial outbreaks. These results have significant implications for public health policy and the development of effective strategies to mitigate the spread of airborne pathogens across different environments.

Deep neural networks are transforming the landscape of anomaly detection and classification, yet these models frequently lack transparency in explaining their decisions. Although they excel in identifying patterns within data, the reasoning behind their performance remains unclear. This limitation hinders their widespread adoption in areas like scientific discovery and safety-critical systems. To address this issue, we focus on uncertainty quantification methods that can evaluate both the reliability of input data and the probability of accurate predictions. We specifically examine machine learning techniques for solving partial differential equations and trained models, including those based on neural networks. These methods enable the assessment of solution and prediction uncertainty. To effectively compare these techniques, we outline a standardized machine learning benchmark involving eight diverse test cases, spanning simple and complex domains. This benchmark consists of: (a) a data efficiency problem with a well-defined solution, (b) an equation with unknown parameters, (a) a missing data problem, (d) a prediction of a physical process from noisy data, (e) a prediction of a physical process from data alone, (f) a prediction of a physical process from limited data, (g) a prediction of a physical process from data and a trained model, and (h) a prediction of a physical process from limited data and a trained model. This benchmark enables a comprehensive evaluation of different uncertainty methods. Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same degree for sufficiently high exponents. Additionally, specific conditions are identified to determine when the symbolic and power series behave equivalently for all integer exponents k>=s.
Using an exact partition function, we analyze a unitary matrix model based on a single plaquette configuration at a finite $N$ for both the SU($N$) and U($N$) symmetries.

Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications, such as automotive navigation systems. Ensuring the reliable operation of these models under abnormal input conditions is a significant challenge. This research proposes an innovative method to validate the activation range supervision technique used to maintain model robustness, by examining and limiting the input data distribution to prevent errors caused by hardware malfunctions.

The European Central Bank's definition of clearing or netting has far-reaching effects on a nation's economy. By reducing the number of transactions that need to be settled between companies, netting can be used to prevent the spread of financial crises. This paper delves into the fundamental concepts behind netting and presents a novel approach to identifying the optimal way to clear debts between businesses, which can be used by financial institutions to stop the spread of financial crises. Additionally, this paper demonstrates how the national authorities in Romania are utilizing this approach on a large scale.

Building upon the Jordanian twist concept, we have derived a generalized version. The generalized version, modified in the $r$-symmetrized format, meets the requirements for a 2-cocycle. Additionally, we have obtained specific formulae for its associated star product and twisted coproduct. Furthermore, we have established that our generalized version is equivalent to 1-coboundary, thus confirming its format. We have also identified specific 0-cocycles that correspond to its 1-coboundary 1-cocycles format.

We build a unified vocabulary space across multiple languages using the concept of cluster consistency. This approach ensures that words from different languages which belong to the same group have similar meanings in terms of semantics. We start by forming clusters based on the nearest neighbors in each language to create mappings between languages. These groups can also be seen as a form of dimension reduction, where the number of groups is much smaller than the total number of words. Next, we evaluate our method on various semantic tasks in English and groups of languages, including tasks like clustering, dimensionality reduction, and learning relationships between languages. Our results indicate that our space construction is effective and efficient, especially when working with more than two languages.

The initial findings from the 5.44 TeV Xe-Xe collisions reveal that pions, kaons, protons, and $\phi$ mesons behave in a manner consistent with 2012 Pb-Pb collision data and 2016 Pb-Pb collision data.  By comparing data to various theoretical models, including TU3, EPOS LHC, and AMPT, we observe that they generally reproduce our findings well.  Notably, in the case of protons, a more in-depth analysis of baryon-to-meson ratios in midrapidity regions shows an increase in this ratio with rising $p_{\rm T}$, a ratio that is higher in Xe-Xe collisions than in lower-energy p-p collisions for $p_{\rm T} > 6$ TeV/c.  Furthermore, our ratio indicates a possible reduction in the proton radial flow, a finding that contradicts current expectations.  Additionally, our data on proton elliptic flow ($v_2$) are in line with $p$-p collision data and provide a basis for research into proton $v_2$ suppression.  On the subject of mesons, our analysis of pions and kaons in $p_{\rm T}$ regions beyond 6 TeV/c reveals an apparent decrease in their mass dependence on transverse momentum, a phenomenon that contradicts expected behavior.
